title: Fully Human Antibody Halts Aggressive Prostate Cancer Spread in Preclinical Study
excerpt: Researchers at Sweden's Umeå University developed a drug made entirely from human proteins that stopped both tumor growth and metastasis through a novel mechanism, raising hopes for men with advanced disease.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A fully human antibody halted tumor growth and metastasis in aggressive prostate cancer models.
  • The drug targets oncogenic TβRI signaling, differing from current treatment mechanisms.
  • Being made of human proteins, it may have fewer side effects than existing therapies.
  • Safety studies and regulatory approvals are needed before clinical trials can start.
  • Research may extend the drug's application to other solid tumors beyond prostate cancer.

Study published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy
  • A fully human antibody developed at Umeå University blocked both tumor growth and metastatic spread in preclinical models of aggressive prostate cancer
  • The drug works through a novel mechanism targeting oncogenic TβRI signaling, a biological route different from existing treatments
  • Because it is made entirely of human proteins, researchers believe the antibody may carry a lower risk of side effects than current therapies
  • Safety studies and regulatory approval in Europe or the US are still required before clinical trials can begin in patients

A team of researchers in Sweden has developed a new antibody drug that stopped aggressive prostate cancer from growing and spreading in laboratory models, marking a potential step forward for men who face one of the deadliest forms of the disease.

The study, published in the journal Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, was led by Maréne Landström, professor of pathology at the Department of Medical Biosciences at Umeå University. The drug is a fully human antibody, meaning it is composed entirely of human proteins, which researchers say makes it better suited for therapeutic use in patients.

A New Line of Attack Against Metastasis

> **"While most tumors grow slowly and pose little immediate threat, a subset of patients develop an aggressive form that spreads beyond the prostate, most commonly to the lymph nodes and bones."**

Prostate cancer is among the most commonly diagnosed cancers in men worldwide. While most tumors grow slowly and pose little immediate threat, a subset of patients develop an aggressive form that spreads beyond the prostate, most commonly to the lymph nodes and bones. Once the cancer metastasizes, treatment options narrow and survival rates drop sharply.

The new antibody targets oncogenic TβRI signaling, a biological pathway that drives cancer cell growth, invasiveness, and metastatic spread. This mechanism of action differs from existing approaches, which the researchers believe could also reduce the risk of side effects.

"The new drug has been developed to prevent metastasis, and we are very pleased and proud that we have been able to identify the mechanisms that drive cancer cell growth, invasiveness and metastatic spread."

— Maréne Landström, Professor of Pathology, Umeå University

In preclinical experiments, the antibody successfully halted both tumor growth and metastatic spread in an aggressive form of prostate cancer. The results confirmed that the treatment performed as intended, an important validation before moving toward clinical use.

From Lab to Clinic: What Comes Next

Despite the promising results, Landström cautioned that several stages remain before the drug could benefit patients. Additional safety studies are required, and the treatment must receive regulatory approval from authorities in Europe or the United States before human trials can begin.

The development of the antibody involved collaboration with drug development specialists at the SciLifeLab Drug Discovery and Development Platform, support from the Umeå Biotech Incubator, and funding from MetaCurUm Biotech AB, a biotechnology company based in Umeå.

Beyond Prostate Cancer

The research team is already exploring whether the same approach could work against other types of solid tumors, potentially broadening the drug's impact beyond prostate cancer.

Next Steps for Clinical Application
›Conduct additional safety studies.
›Obtain regulatory approval in Europe or the US.
›Initiate human clinical trials.
›Explore applications for other solid tumors.

"The next step is to investigate whether this treatment can also be used against other types of solid tumors. We hope that our work will ultimately contribute to the development of a new cancer drug that can benefit patients," Landström said.

For the estimated 1.4 million men diagnosed with prostate cancer globally each year, including a rising number in India and among Indian diaspora communities, the study offers a glimpse of what the next generation of cancer therapy could look like, though the road from laboratory promise to bedside reality remains long.
